summary: Diamond Head Light on Oahu: lit 1 July 1899, rebuilt in concrete in 1918, automated in the 1920s, and closed to visitors as Coast Guard property.

structures.note: present tower completed 1918 at $6,109 (Coast Guard's history)

1899 forty-foot iron frame built by Honolulu Iron Works; the Coast Guard's history says it was 'never installed', while LighthouseFriends and the 1898 Senate report describe it on the site; masonry base built 1899 (LighthouseFriends); dismantled after 1918 (LighthouseFriends)
frame bungalow, 28 by 46 feet (Commissioner's report, fiscal 1922)

access.note: Coast Guard property; grounds, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends); the USLHS record says not open to the public.

events.note: Wooden lookout tower built to watch for ships (Coast Guard's history; LighthouseFriends dates the lookout to 1878)
Lookout established on the seaward slope; John Charles Petersen first watchman (LighthouseFriends)
SS Miowera aground off Diamond Head, night of 2 October 1893; freed after six weeks (LighthouseFriends; Coast Guard's history)
China runs aground near the crater; the Coast Guard's history ties it to the iron tower
Hawaiian government orders iron tower material; the Pacific Commercial Advertiser reports it on 4 December 1897 (quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Senate committee inspects the new iron tower on 31 March 1898 and reports that it needs a stone and cement tower (LighthouseFriends; PCA 12 August 1898)
E. B. Thomas contracted in January 1899 to build the masonry tower for $1,170 (LighthouseFriends)
First lit 1 July 1899 (LighthouseFriends); the Coast Guard's history gives 1899
Third-order Fresnel lens built by Barbier and Benard (Coast Guard's history)
Captain A. Christian stricken with paralysis and blindness on 23 December 1899; dies later (LighthouseFriends)
Diamond Head Charlie fined $50 for striking Keeper Neilsen; dismissed and rehired within months (LighthouseFriends)
Floor added 14 feet above the ground, windows made, telephone lines installed (Coast Guard's history)
Lighthouse Board takes control of all aids to navigation in the Hawaiian Islands (LighthouseFriends)
Incandescent oil vapor system installed (Coast Guard's history)
Efficiency pennant awarded to the station; John Kaukaliu named (Lighthouse Service Bulletin, 1912)
Commissioner's report lists Diamond Head among lights changed from fixed to flashing or occulting (fiscal 1915)
Growing cracks found in the old tower on inspection (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper Kaukaliu found paralyzed at the top of the tower on 6 October; dies eight days later (LighthouseFriends, citing the Honolulu Star-Bulletin)
Funds allocated for a new light (Coast Guard's history)
Present concrete tower completed at a cost of $6,109; old lantern moved onto a temporary frame during the work (Coast Guard's history; LighthouseFriends)
Characteristic changed from fixed to group occulting (Coast Guard's history); the 1915 report already lists the change
Keeper's dwelling completed; frame bungalow (Coast Guard's history; Commissioner's report, fiscal 1922)
LighthouseFriends gives 1923 as the year the station was automated
Lighthouse automated (Coast Guard's history)
Light station turned over to the Coast Guard (Coast Guard's history; LighthouseFriends)
Rear Admiral Benjamin Engel moves into the dwelling, which has since housed the commanders of the Fourteenth Coast Guard District (LighthouseFriends)
Placed on the National Register of Historic Places (Coast Guard's history; NRHP 80001282)

corrections.why: The concrete tower in the record is the 1918 tower (Coast Guard's history: present lighthouse completed 1918 at $6,109). The 1899 tower was an iron frame with masonry; it was replaced.
Coast Guard property; grounds, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends); USLHS record: not open to the public.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first light was 1899 (Coast Guard's history; LighthouseFriends; USLHS record). The 1917 dates in Wikidata and OpenStreetMap refer to the concrete tower, funded in 1917 and completed in 1918 (Coast Guard's history).

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left open: (1) the lookout, 1856 (Coast Guard's history) or 1878 (LighthouseFriends); (2) the keepers: the Coast Guard's history gives Kaukaliu 1899-1914, Reid 1915-1917 and 1918-1919, Toomey 1919-1924, against the USLHS roster (Neilsen 1899-1904; Kaukaliu 1904-1916; Reid 1916-1920; Toomey 1920-1923); the roster is used, and the Coast Guard's lines are named in the story; (3) the characteristic change, 1915 (Commissioner's report, fiscal 1915) or 1918 (Coast Guard's history); (4) automation, 1923 (LighthouseFriends) or 1924 (Coast Guard's history); (5) the 1899 lit date rests on LighthouseFriends for '1 July'; the Coast Guard's history gives only 1899. Hawaiian newspapers: the Library of Congress returned HTTP 520 for every Diamond Head query in the 1899 window; only the 12 August 1898 pages (PCA p. 6; Hawaiian Gazette p. 5) were read. The 1916 death date and the Star-Bulletin citation are LighthouseFriends', not read. The NRHP nomination (80001282) is a 3.7 KB OCR result that is not legible; it was not used beyond the listing date from the Coast Guard's history. The Commissioner's 1922 OCR reads 'bv' for 'by'; the evidence quote keeps the OCR form. The Commissioner's 1922 list (p. 731) of lights changed from incandescent oil vapor to electric incandescent is not used: the year it covers is not clear from the snippet. Focal height: the USLHS record gives 146 feet above mean high water (44.5 m); Wikidata gives 45 m, OSM gives 147 (probably feet). The record's 44.8 m is not used. Characteristic: not stated in any source read here; the record's 'Oc(2) W 10s' and 'Oc(2) WR 10s' are not used. The Transpac finish-line statement is LighthouseFriends' and was not checked elsewhere. LighthouseFriends is a copyrighted site: facts are paraphrased; no quotation is taken from it. Fact-check 2026-10-22 (sentence-by-sentence against the Coast Guard's history (archived copy), LighthouseFriends, the Pacific Commercial Advertiser and Hawaiian Gazette of 12 Aug 1898, the Commissioner's reports for 1915, 1920 and 1922, the 1912 Lighthouse Service Bulletin, and the USLHS record). Changed in the story: the iron frame is now reported with the Coast Guard's 'never installed' against LighthouseFriends and the 1898 Senate report, which describe it on the site; the China's 'near the crater' is footnoted to LighthouseFriends; the Coast Guard's 1914 end date for Kaukaliu is stated beside the roster's 1916, and the Coast Guard's Reid and Toomey stints are added as rows without a person slug; the lookout's date (1856 against 1878) is stated as a disagreement; the 1915 and 1918 characteristic change is stated as a disagreement; 'the best views' and 'only obstructed views' are replaced by LighthouseFriends' 'good, distant views' and 'obstructed views are possible'; the unsourced directive to stay off the grounds is removed; the 'closed' status is cited to LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record; the Star-Bulletin is attributed as a source LighthouseFriends lists, not as read. Printed pages added: Commissioner 1915 p. 8, 1920 p. 54, 1922 p. 42 (the corpus page index reads each, with scan pages). The 1912 pennant list is confirmed in the Bulletin's efficiency-pennant table (District 19, Diamond Head, John Kaukaliu). Still open: the characteristic change (1915 or 1918) and the automation year (1923 or 1924); the lit date rests on LighthouseFriends' 1 July 1899 (the Coast Guard gives only 1899); the 1899 Hawaiian newspapers were not reached (the researcher's Library of Congress queries returned HTTP 520) and were not re-tried. Focal height: the USLHS record gives 146 ft above mean high water (44.5 m); used in the facts. Keeper names: LighthouseFriends prints 'Niel C. Nielson' and 'Charles Peterson'; the story uses the roster's Neil C. Neilsen and LighthouseFriends' 'Diamond Head Charlie'. Living-people check: Rear Admiral Engel is named in his public role (1967) only.
